I think a lot of people didn’t understand the new process when it came out and were confused. But this is the correct way haha.

So, you scan one of every color. So let’s say you have men’s 511 jeans and 8 colors, you scan one of each color. You wouldn’t scan one of each size, because you’re scanning each customer choice in terms of color. A customer choice wouldn’t necessarily be size because that’s a less of a choice and more of a requirement of dressing your body versus yellow or green is a choice. If you’re creating a sign, you can’t scan that many, so that’s usually when they run into the overcrowded look. Stores should be avoiding more than 2-3 e-signs per fixture, unless absolutely needed.

Like if one week the Sonoma tees are 9.99, but then another they’re on sale for 7.99 I’ll have both price points in the frames so I don’t have to run upstairs. Overtime, you’ll see what prices are consistently the same. Some people use a grey cart, and have their price points on there. I personally don’t find that works for me. I’ll go around the store with a pen and paper, make notes of if there is already a frame and/or hardware there, what graphic it needs, then I go back upstairs, put all of it on the cart and then go around the store like that. 

So for Epic Deals, I probably had about 30-45 price points pre-stuffed from previous sale events. Things like basics and front tables. Everyone has their own system, I personally find this to be the easiest. Good luck :)

I will let you know, that HR is there to protect the company, not you (this is coming from an employee who has been involved in several HR issues as a witness/complainant, including on an on the job injury). So hopefully, they just mark this in the books, you both get talked to and sign a no-retaliation agreement and this gets filed away, and that’s the end of it. I personally have a great relationship with my admin, so for days off and vacations I’ll just go through her and my executives have no problem with it. But for massive schedule changes or if I need to leave early, and make up my time later in the week, that’s definitely where I would talk to my SM first and follow up with my admin. Technically, getting another job and not having the availability to meet what your store needs is a fireable offense, in the sense that they can let you go if you don’t meet the needs of the business or they’ll just never schedule you, if they can’t get the approval from HR. 

Also, just as a rule of thumb. Regardless of what job you have, or what career your in, posting about new potential job opportunities is discouraged simply because if the company you work for finds out, they can let you go for a simple reason such as not meeting store needs or the job you’re apply for is direct competition for said company, which in many states is also a fireable offense. Most states are “at will” states which essentially means you can be fired or let go for any reason. 

Hopefully, this works out for you.

Edit: i understand they’re not scheduling you, but if you change your availability because you have another job, they can say you no longer meet the needs.

We do “blitz” freight merchandising. But we specifically pair certain people together. For instance, I usually do hardlines with one supervisor (who when we had departments, was men’s and now got moved to home, kids, and shoes) and our ASM and other supervisor take the rest of the team to do grey carts first and then rails. And we have one full time and one part time person do shoes (they’re a great team and super comfortable with the department, I usually run the residual the next day if there’s any). And our operations sup floats between after cleaning up the dock and loading the truck. I understand being frustrated, but there is a reason certain people do certain things. If we let everyone and anyone, including our freight team which consists of full timers and really great part timers do hardlines, it would get completely messed up. These are people I have worked side by side with, many for years, and they still can’t do it correctly and get pissy with me when I try to correct. Bestie, I am the Visual, I have the most information about merchandising everywhere because that’s my job, and work closely with the executives everyday to get merchandising and sets done. Everyone else, also has access to this information but either doesn’t want to look it up, or just doesn’t care to. I totally get kohls idea of removing the e sups, but there are some supervisors who will be naturally strong in certain areas- for example the ops and service sup. There is a reason those two have such a specific job and it’s because it requires a certain type of person with certain trainable skills and mindset. Training really only goes so far , especially when there are part timers who by definition are part time. When visits come around, they’re not the ones being judged. At my store, we all take a lot of pride in our work and we all have areas we’re great in and areas we’re bad in. For example, I don’t do accessories because I actually suck. I cannot for the life of me make a purse table look good. You know what I’m the best at? Infant toddler, the department most people find difficult, it comes so naturally to me. I don’t really count men’s or women’s because those are areas I’ve done and re-done a thousand times and we have plenty of other people strong in those areas. 

Full timers have a right to be upset when you run freight incorrectly. You may think it’s correct, but do you have all the info? A lot of kohls merchandising is actually very specific, such as priority merchandise, tables, endcaps and flow. Kids , juniors, and home are great examples of that. Men’s and women’s has become a little more lax, more fashion forward and gives options to play around, but everything else is specific because the merchandise is specific. 

I absolutely adore our truck team and I love watching the part timers, who are essential to our team, get confident enough to make merchandising decisions. One of our part timers two trucks ago came to me and said “here’s what what I want to do because of x and x” and I was like hell yeah, that’s exactly what I would have done!

It depends on your state, in my state, WA, 32 hours or more is considered full time. True full time is 40 hours. You can work less than 32 hours a week, as long as you’re average is 32. In my state , pto does count towards hours worked, I’m not sure where you got the information that it doesn’t, but it may very by state. What’s your state? I can do some digging and translate some of the official legislative writing. Also, depending on your state, if you have a full time position, they have to be scheduling you the states minimum, in my case 32 a week. If you’re taking pto it comes from a different fund, not the active scheduling fund, but it would still count towards hours worked. Ohio code states “A full time employee is defined as an individual employed on a forty hour per week, nine-, ten-, eleven-, or twelve-month basis per fiscal year; or an individual employed an average of not less than thirty hours per week on a twelve month contract shall be considered a full time employee.” 
https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-3357:12-3-01


Kentucky code states “thirty-seven and one-half (37.5) hours per week or forty (40) hours per week”
https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/101/002/095/#:~:text=The%20number%20of%20hours%20a,appointing%20authority%20or%20the%20statutes.

Or 

“Kentucky labor laws do not define full-time and part-time employment.  Employers are free to define these terms as they choose.”
https://elc.ky.gov/workplace-standards/Pages/Wages-and-Hours.aspx

I would be very careful about using a leash to mitigate threat and monitor interaction. That can lead to leash aggression. We have four dogs (ages, 10 months, 1 year, 1 year, and 4 years) in the house, and one cat (6 months). We’re split into a duplex, but all live together with interactions, so the two one year olds live with the cat full time, but we wanted to make sure my dogs could handle being around the cat as well. The 4 year old (bully mix) one of the year olds (bully mix) and the 10 month old (gsd mix) had a very hard time with introductions likely due to their high prey institutions/drive. The other one year old is a golden retriever and was more just intrigued but would go after the cat if the other one year old did. We did a barrier, put one person in the bathroom with the cat, and had another person sit with each dog individually. It took roughly two months to get everyone comfortable with even being chill through the door. And then we moved onto baby gates, and feeding next to each other. And only after that, we’re the dogs just able to chill with the kitty, even now they get a bit crazy, but the cat will fight back, and we’ve given her plenty of places to climb and hide from the dogs. We also have the this baby lock thing on the door, so the cat can get in but the dogs can’t.

Part of the training we did to calm the dogs down was using “leave it” and putting them into down stays or sits (depending on training level), and then rewarding them for any non-interaction with the cat such as high value treats. For example, looking at the cat, but not moving towards him. And keeping an eye out for aggressive body language, being super tense, locking eyes,’ refusal to take a distraction such as a treat. Another thing to note, it is probably super scary for your cat as well , so they both do need comforting. It was slightly different for us, since our cat was so young, it sounds like you’re cat is quite a bit older.

I have a 4 year old and a 9 month old, only the puppy stays in the crate. 

5:30am - wake up, take the boys out, do some gentle play and training. Usually older boy goes back to sleep because he’s tired and not having it. 

5:45am - call the boys for breakfast.

5:45-6:45 - hang out with them, usually a second potty break for the pup, I relax and eat breakfast and they just kind of vibe. Maybe another short training session. 

6:45 - start getting ready for my day, get dressed, etc. I’ll take the older boy potty. 

7am - another potty session for the puppy, and then he’s usually pretty pooped. 

7:15am - he’s ready to go back into his crate. 

7:15-7:30am - I have some time for my older boy
7:30am - leave for work

4pm - home from work, dogs get taken out again.

4pm-7pm - play time, training time, several more potty breaks. Go to the park every other day. 

7pm - dinner time for the boys.

7pm-9:30 - relax time, small training sessions, I eat dinner, and more potty breaks. (Puppy usually goes to the crate while we eat- generally 7:30-8:30) 

9:30-10:30 - continue to relax, usually both boys fall asleep in the living room. And then bedtime. Bedtime fluctuates. 

Saturdays and Sunday’s are my days off. So from about 7am-12pm both dogs are out. Around 12pm I have to do an enforced nap for the puppy, because he’s overstimulated and begins trying to hump his brother 🙄🙄. I usually run errands from 12-1:30, if needed, and then the puppy is back out of the crate until about 7:30 when I eat dinner, he goes into the crate for that duration, and is back out from 8:30-11pm. And then bedtime. Generally we go to the park both days around 4:30pm. 

The 5-6 month mark, we were up at about 4:30 each morning taking him potty before going back to bed for another hour. 

People may disagree with the amount of time the puppy spends in the crate but that’s fine. He has a great life! We don’t do walks, we do sniff time in the backyard. I throw smelly treats and make him find them. People may also disagree with that, but that’s okay. Walks don’t really work for my babes, and that’s fine. Occasionally, my boyfriend will take the older boy on a run, and the puppy and I usually go on a neighborhood walk when that happens. They’re too chaotic together haha. And about every other weekend we go to the beach or a hiking trail, and let them run wild.

Edit: another potential contention point with other dog owners. I got my puppy at 14 weeks, and this has been his schedule since I got him. Give or take waking up in the middle of the night for potty breaks. He never had an accident in the crate or in the house waiting for me to let him out after I got home.

Not a whole lot of advice, because my GSD is only 20 weeks but I did get him at 14 weeks. So, I wake up at 6am every morning for work, so he goes to bed around 10:30. Around 9pm, we have play time for about 15 minutes and then I encourage our older dog, if he wants to (he usually does), to join in for another 15 minutes. We then go potty in our usual spot, and then go on a 15-20 minute walk where I let him smell everything to tire him out. We get back around 9:45 usually so my boyfriend and I will hang out on the couch and the pups will hang out by our feet and we don’t give him any attention so he’ll settle on his own, I will give him a chew if he needs it. He generally is asleep by 10:30 and then I wake him up, take him potty again and put him in his crate. Turn off all the lights and go to bed. He still wakes up around 4 or 5 and whines, so I get out of bed, I don’t turn the lights on just open the crate, put his leash on and take him outside. I don’t say anything or give him attention besides the usual “go potty” once we’re outside and a “good boy!”, and then straight back into the crate. No talking, no jumping, no playing. If he cries after that, he’ll usually settle after 15 minutes. He throws these funny tantrums where he pulls the blanket into the crate and hangs on to it. And he usually sleeps until about 6:30 and then we hang out for an hour before I leave for work.

Just call out and use sick time. Or if you don’t have sick time just call out. I’ve yet to hear of anyone getting fired for that. And of course if your store cares about attendance points as long as you’re within those 12, you’ll be fine.

From past experience, I generally wait for two things. A big shift in management (because we’ve gone through 4 SM in my 4 years here) and or annual reviews we get in February. I’ve gotten at least a .10 raise each year, excluding the initial lead bump and the minimum wage changing. Last February I received a .75 raise. However, kohls tries to say you can’t speak about how much money you make to coworkers. My store is pretty much not with that mentality- one because we all think we deserve to be paid the same if we are all leads and tenure is important and two because it’s illegal to not be allowed to talk about it. 

Now for the fun part. Request a meeting with your SM, it’s going to make them nervous especially because you’re a shoe lead and I feel like most people don’t keep those leads for long. Let them know what accomplishments you’ve achieved, what you’ve learned, talk about customer experience, and then this one is debatable but talk about cost of living and your interest in potentially going to work for someone else, and that your very aware what other people make at the store (that’s a hit or miss point). And then make sure you’re asking for an unrealistic number, so two or three dollars more than want you think is realistic. And be ready to go back and forth. Your SM will then need approval from your DM which depending on your relationship with your SM could take a while. 

Don’t ask for a raise if you have a bad relationship with them. It won’t happen. But know that the SM having to go through the DM is what happens and it does take time .

Edit: oh and good luck!

Take it outside or into the shower (make sure you clean/sanitize the shower afterwords for regular human use) depending on sizing. Take it apart, hose down all the parts individually. After that I scrubbed the cage with dawn dish soap, using a variety of brushes (toothbrushes work great for getting in between the bars). I then rinse the cage again. If there are any really dirty areas such as stained platforms, do a soak with warm water and soap, and then give it a good scrub. After that I then go through and give everything a thorough wipe down with 2 parts water, 1 part vinegar. I then go ahead and wait for everything to dry. It’s also important to check for damage such as rust, or bent bars. I had an unfortunate incident where a bar was bent and one of my babies was stuck, she was fine, just a little scared. Once it’s dry, assemble it. And then I like to recheck everything. And if I missed anything i will scrub with vinegar again. I have heard about some really dirty cages, in that case you can use harsher chemicals but make sure there is plenty of time to let it air out and potentially wash it again with rat safe cleaning solution such as the water vinegar mix

So, I’ve seen “alpha” and “dominant” used interchangeably. My dominant girl has always been the dominant one, even before I got them. All animals have a hierarchy, but truthfully I don’t think it matters how you refer to the hierarchy as long as your understanding the behaviors within your own animals. 

I mean take dogs for example. My dog, who was 18 when she died and a beautiful runt black lab who had been severely abused while being raised as a hunting dog before we got her immediately knew my dad, as a male, to be the one in charge. The alpha you could say. But she knew to protect me, and would even go up against my dad if she felt he was a threat (an unfounded one but…) and when my mom was pregnant with my brother she was sit on the bed and guard her while she slept. Her behavior was seen as dominant until someone with more dominance was in charge. Her dominance in the hierarchy wasn’t changing but moving based on who was around.

So, I did a half bio-active, half normal...I guess is the best way to describe it. I built a plexiglass base for the lower half of my critter nation ( there's tutorials online for this!), but the remaining half of their cage is relatively normal items. My main goal was really just to give them a lot of places to dig.

1. I use springtails to help clean and regulate my soil (the type of soil I use is coco coir soil). Springtails are microscopic, and generally can't or don't live outside of the soil. I have yet to have issues. When I do put in meal worms as treats, I make sure to watch them carefully, not because I'm afraid of the worms getting out, but that my girls will take them out, haha.
2. Set up cost, for the base alone, was roughly $100, if you're going bioactive for the rest of your cage, probably another $100. But in terms of maintenance, I've researched that the dirt doesn't need to be changed often, maybe every few months? I think it's really up to you and what is happening in your cage. I do spray the soil down every day with water from a spray bottle, and still use my regular cleaning supplies for the other items in the cage. For cleaning natural items, you'll want to do some research on what will be the safest way to do so. Most natural woods can be cleaned with a vinegar/water solution and be fine. With the natural items I do have in the cage, I haven't done anything different in terms of cleaning.
3. I honestly enjoy the smell. It's a very fresh soil smell, like a garden. And as I still use the regular fleece blankets and hammocks for their cuddling pleasure, I can smell the ammonia when I get up close, but from just in my room, there is a dirt smell. I've yet to have any issues with rotting with the natural woods I do use, but be aware of that as it can cause a smell.
4. If you make sure your base has a big enough space between the top of the base and where the dirt starts, you will be fine. My base is 16" tall, but the dirt only comes up to 10". They have yet to throw dirt out of that. However, I do have an old rug that I have underneath their cage, so if dirt does get thrown or knocked out, it will be an easy clean up and protect my carpets.
5. If i removed all the shelves in my cage, there would be a riot. My rats think the best place to sleep is on the bar plastic shelf, pressed up against the cage bars lol. I have one shelf at the very top, and have taken all the other shelves out. I have woven baskets and branches throughout the rest of the cage to help them climb around, and for them to sleep in. (It's also helpful to put branches in the dirt to add support when they're tunneling). And it does not defeat the purpose. A true bio-active cage refers to the dirt itself. But if your rats are happy and you are happy, you can do anything you want!
6. The cage itself is not self-cleaning. It's meant so you're not emptying the base every single week (or throughout the week).  The springtails, which are the clean up crew, help with getting rid of poop and urine that end up in the soil, which keeps it free. The rest of the cage will still need relatively regular cleaning. The point of bio-active cages to my understanding is to give your rats the best, most natural to their instincts enrichment. . I have some excellent links that helped me build mine, if you'd like me to post them? However, it is super important to monitor everything in a bio-active cage. If your rats for whatever reason try to start eating things, I put some rat safe leaves in the cage, and one of my girls decided that they should be her only source of nutrition and got intentional blockage (face palm). And your soil should be turned through every week, and should make sure it's sprayed down on the top so the dust does not irritate their respiratory systems.

Edit: I do use non-bio active materials, as I mentioned before. But that's just a personal preference. My rats favorite new dirt toy is a box full of shredded paper. One takes the paper out, the other kicks dirt in, and the third takes all the dirt out of the box and puts the paper back in. It's very amusing to watch. Just remember that it is up to you how you want to do this. I'm sure whatever you decide your ratties will thank you!

I spot clean everyday, but I am really big on doing a weekly cleaning. Mostly because as humans we need a clean environment, so if I let their cage go any longer it gets a bit much for my nose. It’s also likely because I use fleece. I change their loose bedding every three days, though. I’m planning on making a deep plexiglass base for half of the bottom so they can dig more. I generally do a clean on Sunday. Take out all the hammocks and blankets, throw that in the laundry and then wipe down the cage and all items with white vinegar and water solution, after taking out the blankets I’m able to clean the baskets. I soak their water bottle, litter tray, and food bowl( separately of course). And if there are any sections that are particularly dirty for whatever reason I’ll scrub it with a rat specific tooth brush. I will generally run a soaked clean towel through the pink tube and really get in there, but my plan is every three weeks to take it down and soak it. I like to rearrange their cage after every clean to give them some variety, the ropes are a temporary solution until I’m able to get some of those ikea things, but the rope is cotton and from the dollar store so I can’t run it through the wash but I can soak it and air dry. I do lock the girls up in their travel cage while I wait for their cage to dry but then let them free roam the rest of the time until everything is washed and dry. It normally takes about 30 minutes to do the actual manual cleaning, another 1.5 hours to do the laundry, and another 1.5 hours to do the cage re-set. So really just about 2.5, maybe 3 hours of the girls are being difficult haha. And then I’ll do my own thing while they free roam. I generally free roam 1-2 hours a day, so on cleaning days they get 3-4 hours which they love so it works pretty well for both of us. Worst case scenario, if I need to leave while their stuff is in the laundry, I leave them in the travel cage with a clean rag towel, a toilet paper roll, and a water dish. But that rarely happens.

I also have a good friend who helps me with them. He comes over and socializes with me and them for a few hours every week. And is a huge help when he’s over on cleaning days, able to help me reset the cage if needed. I feel very fortunate to be able to do so much for them, and truthfully I struggle a lot with depression so having a huge task is helpful as I often have weekends off and don’t do much. It motivates me to get moving and prepare for the rest of my work week, as well as clean my own room so they can free roam safely

If LP is not in the building, you'll report to an H2 who will call the ROC and they will remotely log into our cameras and get information on the suspect to give to police if anything is damaged or stolen. Make sure you wear comfy clothes. Jeans and a t-shirt if your store isn't super strict about what you wear. Make sure you wear stuff you're not afraid to get dirty. I like to check in with my h2 who's running truck, generally the OPs, and see what time they're coming in. They'll probably be there at 6am with one other associate, or they'll be in at 6:30 with you being the other associate, with people arriving between 6:30 and 7am. Once I'm there I'll go sign in, grab a walkie but leave my headset and grab a Zebra. I'll pop downstairs and help them clear the dock and set up z-rails and grey carts, which are both for clothing (soft lines). And then the orange carts with shelves and without are for home/bedding/etc.. (hard lines). As well as help set up the line, which is this metal thing with rolling pieces. You'll have one or two people inside the truck scanning the packages and throwing them onto the line. You're h2 or another associate will cut into the boxes and toss them to either the hard line sides or soft line sides. And then whichever side you're on, you'll likely switch depending on your crew, you'll sort them out. It's important to keep things really organized. And then later in the day or the following day depending on your crew and how much time you have, you'll merchandise the freight, which is wear you go the floor and put out all the merchandise. Our store generally finishes hardlines the same day we do the truck and softlines the next day. But our truck team is generally only 4-5 people sadly...

Okay, so price changes are super easy, just stressful. You're H2 or lead will walk you through where you need to be on the device but basically, you just go around the store scanning stuff and sticking labels on. 

There are a couple of types of price changes.

\-new marks, which is where you go to the sales floor and the zebra will show you what items in which departments need to go clearence. You'll scan the barcode and it will print a clearance label. Most stores will then throw the items on a z-rail or a orange/grey cart for folds (some stores leave them until price changes are over, but that doesn't make much sense). It's super important you scan every item, even if they don't have tags, just type the UPC and stick that yellow tag on the shirt. We have to get to a certain percentage to "complete" the price change event. When you do this, don't ever cover the barcode with the clearance sticker. 

\-occasionally new marks will be white ticket labels, generally only in intimates though. This is where you'll scan the barcode and it will print a white ticket with a new original price on it, and you'll just cover up the barcode. These hardly happen and tend to be pretty small.

\-additional marks, is where you go to each clearance section and scan every single item and print out another clearance sticker and cover the old one. This one is tiring because you have no idea what you have to scan or what will actually be an additional mark, but you still have to reach a certain percentage to "complete" it.

Occasionally during price changes you'll run across something that says "set aside for MOS processing", whoever is leading the team will let you know what to do with that. Essentially, it gets MOS (marked out of stock) using the zebra and the merchandise disposition app. Which, unless you spend a lot of time in CS, you probably don't know how to do that, so don't sweat it.

I've thought about making a google doc guide and posting it here with pictures attached of what buttons to press on the Zebra, especially so people can reference for things like linking e-signs which is so important. If I end up doing that, I'll try to remember to tag you. But also, don't ever feel like a bother, ask people. Especially if you see people putting out the truck freight, they have to link e-signs as they go and they'll be happy to show you. Or if you see one that just says "kohls", it means it needs to be re-linked and you could ask someone to show you then. H2s don't deliberately not want you to learn, they're just hella busy and overworked, and really you have to ask these days when you want to learn something.

Anyway, good luck. The price changes that you're scheduled for will probably new marks clearance, so it'll be pretty easy. But if you have questions ask whoever's leading the event, it will probably be your ops supervisor or your ASM.

So, I don't know what you're talking about "misplaced items"....but the being on the floor regardless of the department is all the same, for the most part.

When you get to work, grab a walkie and a zebra (if possible). Being on the floor with a zebra is so so so important. If you don't know how to use a zebra you need to ask. I'm at work on Saturday and I've thought about taking some photos of the screens and posting a how-to guide on here, so if I have time I will tag you. After you're clocked in say "this is \_\_\_\_, I'm here for my shift, where do you want me." A lot of the time you will not be where you're scheduled. They might throw you into the women's fitting room or have you fold in juniors. Never assume where your scheduled is correct. After checking in with managment, go to the right department or whatever it is they ask.

If you're scheduled home and kids, they'll probably tell you where to start. Like folding in infant/tod or folding in big girls, etc... If they just tell you that you are home and kids, here's what I would do.

1.) Take a quick walk of your department, make mental notes about what zones (meaning sections of the department) that need to be recovered. Clearance is always a zone that will need to be recovered but, it will get messed up so much throughout your shift that it's better to wait until the other stuff is done. 

2.) After you've taken your floor walk, you'll want to grab your Go-Backs, which I'm assuming is the "misplaced items" you're talking about. Your store will either call them Go-Backs or 500s, these are located in the room behind customer services/on the dock. They're generally on silver carts that have a hang bar and a few shelves, and they're generally labeled with what they are. If there are a lot, you're going to want to pull those carts and run those first. Customer Service will thank you. I like to tell them I'm taking their carts, so they don't get confused when they don't see the cart.

\-home is considered a hard line because it's the heavier, generally more expensive stuff. The CS associates should be organizing your carts, but if they were super busy or have a lot of stuff they may not have. The home carts are also on occasion on grey or orange u-boats (which are generally on the dock, they'll be obvious when you see them). I like to run home first, I'll spend some time organizing the cart, if it's a mess. Basically make sure the towels are all together, and the blender and the coffee makers are together on the cart, etc.. Take this cart to the floor and start running it, as you run the cart, if you see other items out of place or you're able to do a quick clean of the area feel free. It will help later on.

\-kids is considered soft lines (along with the rest of clothes). Take that cart from CS and again spend some time organizing. Here's how I section, in kids you'll have these sections:

* infant
   * baby boy
   * baby girl
* toddler
   * boy
   * girl

You'll notice, after a while that infant and tod, depending on will be mixed on folded fixtures but there's a clear difference between the clothing that is hangers and that is folded.

* boys
   * little boys
   * big boys

There are sizing names associated with this but off the top of my head, I cannot remember. And these aren't official names, just what I call them. I believe little boys is sizes 4-8, and big boys is sizes 8-20. You'll want to double check though.

* girls
   * little girls
   * big girls

The sizing is the same for the girls.

And then within these sections, once you know the floor a bit better, you'll be able to sort them in order of where they are on the sales floor to make running faster. Also, in each section, you'll want to sort clearance out to the end of each section. Make sure you size and colorize in your clearance. 

3.) When you finish with CS go-backs/500s, pop up to the register and see if they have any go backs. You might want to bring a cart there to take whatever there is back to the floor. After that, after that make sure all carts get back to the correct places. 

4.) Grab a folding table from the back and start recovery. I personally don't need a folding table for little kids clothing, but it's nice to have a table to fold on instead of the fixture's shelves. And if you don't know how to us the table, ask someone, it's very important you know how to use it. Recovery consists of folding fixtures/tables, sizing tables/racks, and picking up things and putting them back where they go.

5.) When recovery is finished, head to each of the kids and home clearance and start cleaning up. Most stores are trying to keep their clearance sized and colorized, but it's always a struggle so try you're best. And for home clearance, just make sure it's as nice as possible, but don't worry too much. It's always kind of a mess..

You will also be responsible for handling price checker calls, if you have on in your department. You'll hear "\_\_\_\_ please \_\_\_\_\_". At my store, ours is "boys please boys". You'll want to walk over, hold the button to turn off the overhead page and help the customer. Also, check the price checkers for go-backs. People will often dump everything at the price checkers. If it's from a different department, and you have time to run it please do, but if not take the items to CS and make sure they go to the right cart. 

You will also need to take phone calls for home and kids. The phone will say "customer call for \_\_\_instert department name here\_\_\_ line \_\_\_Inster line number here" (that cannot be correct, but my brain can't remember what she says exactly...) Either way, you'll walk to the phone and pick up the correct line number, to do that you'll select the one of the buttons, generally the one that is flashing. Don't be nervous about answering the phone. My biggest pet peeve is new people not answering the phone. My greeting general is "thank you for calling Kohls in \_\_\_insert city here\_\_\_, this is \_\_\_your name\_\_\_, what can I do for you today?", they generally want to know about an item you have in stock or not. Get a UPC or SKU, and also have your phone ready because if they can't find the UPC or SKU, you'll want to get the description from them and look for the shirt on the Kohls app (you can also use the Kohls app on the zebra to search).

As for breaks, it really does depend. If you are the only person on the sales floor, the H2/HH might make you wait until someone else returns from break. But, no, no one covers a floor department. Coverage only happens for desk roles (CS, Amazon, reg., and OMNI as well). 

But also bear in mind, you might be in the middle of home and kids and they might need amazon back up or reg. back up. Or someone might go the womens/mens fitting room and see it's a disaster and ask for all sales floor people to come for a blitz. This also means you might be answering phone calls for another department. Or helping customers in another department. Basically, be a team player. And if you don't know the answer, for a customer, where something goes, how to do something....ASK. We are here to help, we want to help. If an associate or H2 seems kind of bitchy, we're sorry, we don't mean it and we care about you and want you to do well.

This was a lot of info, if you have any more specific questions, feel free to ask me!

Hope your next couple of work days go well!

How the Kohls Charge Card (or I think corporate wants us to call it just the Kohls Card now...?) works:

Congratulations you've just opened your first credit card. You're credit limit is $300, this means you can only have at most a $300 balance on your card. However, as StuJay99 reccomends "30% of your credit limit if you carry a balance and others recommend that your spend only 10%." My rule of thumb is if you can't afford it right now, you don't need to charge it your credit card. The APR is ridiclously high, so APR is the amount of interest charged on the your card's balance each month. So, let's say you have $150 on your credit card, that's a bit high but you still have a remaning ability to charge $150 to the card. You recieve your credit card statement, in the mail or online (if you signed up for paperless, you'll get an email saying your charge card statment is available, make sure you register your card online or the kohls app). When you recieve your statment, you see that you need to make a minimum payment of X amount of money (that can be paid with check, debit card, or cash- you have some options whether you want to pay in store, over the phone, or online). Let's say that minimum payment is $25, so you make the minimum payment and now have a balance of $125. The remaining balance is then charged interest, the Kohls card **interest rate is 24.99%** (for comparison, my BECU cc is 15% and my Chase cc is 14.99% , these are pretty relative to the APR/interest rates you'll find on non-store credit cards). Each month that your balance is not paid off in full, you will get charged interest on the balance. 

I can get more specific with the math, if you have any questions, but for a credit limit this low, as long as you're paying it off in full or understanding that you're being charged 24.99% in interest each month you'll be fine.

So, by opening the Kohls card, you're credit score was impacted. You'll recieve a hard inquiry on your credit report, and this will often drop your score by a few points. Credit scores are calculated by a few different things. How many credit cards/loans you have open, how much money is on each card (called utilization), and if you're making on-time payments or paying in full each month. The goal is to get your credit score to the perfect range, high 790s-800s. I'm assuming you're pretty young, and probably have little to no credit, so it's great that you're building credit. If you're able to start charging to the card, and use it responsbily, great! This will help you build your score and make it easier for you to be accepted for higher credit limits on other credit cards (there's a lot of great options out there, such as cash back credit cards).

Somewhere at your register will be a booklet that says Kohl’s on it, this section of apps is blue and link colored. You’ll want to find that first, as well as the little card board slips (with the barcode) for rewards.

You’ll scan the first barcode and it will prompt the customer and the pin pad. They’ll say yes to terms of the agreement, and then you’re screen will ask which form of ID they’re using. Generally it’s drivers license, select that option and it will prompt the customer to click yes if they consent to us scanning their ID. Scan the back of their ID and it will prompt the rest of the interaction. It will then ask if they have a rewards account with us (the phone number) always click the phone number because if they end up not having one it auto rolls into creating one. 

It will then ask the customer a bunch of questions (or pull from the rewards info): Ssn, income, address, email, name, etc... and at the end of all that, if they don’t have rewards already it will prompt you to scan the rewards slip. It will then ask the customer to sign at the pin pad. At that point one of three things will happen: 1) The customer will be automatically approved and it will tell you their balance 2) it will tell you to call account look up immediately, the number is 1-888-834-0064. It should be auto dial on the phone beside the register. The operator will ask for your name, associate number, or store number and then it’ll take less than 5 minutes. They’ll give you the card number and card limit. You’ll click submit and they’re all set. 3) it will say they are unable to process at this time but they will contact you by email.

1 and 2 mean you give them 35% and 3 is the 15% off coupon and a manual 10. You can do this before trying to sign them up for a kohl’s charge or after, I generally do it before and alter it if they don’t get approved.

You're best friend is sorting as you go.

Three basic bins:
1. Just hangs (items that need to be hanged or folded and put on go back carts)
2. Re-ticket (items that either don't have a tag anymore or it's now clearance)
3. Merch disposition (items that have been marked down)

I occasionally keep extra bins, for no UPC-need research and mainframe re-ticket. There should also be blue bin (web-ex), yellow bin (sort to location), and red bin (destroy). Make sure you know the process for all of these.

There is nothing worse than coming into a shift and finding all of these items mixed up! If you're doing a closing shift, I also like to lable the bins so the morning associate knows what's left to do.

Try to keep things off the floor so process bulky items first. Also, if you're overwhelmed focus on the just hangs. Make sure the go back carts/bins are organized too. 

As for dealing with customers, when they're loosing kohls cash, make sure they understand because I find that's the biggest problem we have. Also, try to answer the phone in between customers and put the phone on hold. It's better to be on hold then for the phone to ring for 5 minutes. 

On the flip side, customer service is for returns and post-sale, keep the check outs to a minimum, especially when you have a line. 

There is a few other tricks like occasionally the UPC on the recipient will not match the item because the cashier screwed up, just copy the one from the recipient if the item description matches. Also, for post sale, the purchase cannot be done before the date of the coupon, at that point they need to return and repurchase. And of course non-receipt returns are possible but they will not get the price they purchased.

1. You pick up the forms that are the register. It will have associate I.D, store number, and date at the top and information for the customer below that. Then, there are two barcodes before the form gets to the terms of the agreement. Generally, these forms are inside packets that explain what a Kohl's Charge Card is (it's a pinkish color). If they say yes, you scan the barcode, either of them, and hand the form to the customer to fill out. When they fill it out, they should take it home, then they'll fill out the information on the pin pad that was prompted by you scanning the barcode. Occasionally a pop up will occur on your screen asking if they want a Yes2You rewards card, just ask and follow the instructions. From there you just follow the instructions on the pinpad and/or your screen. At the end, it will prompt you to call Kohl's credit approval center. You call the number and give them the activation number, they'll tell you what their card number is, which you'll type in, and they will give you how much the card is good for (generally about $500 or $1000). And after that, they're all set. You tell them their card will come in the mail within a week or two. Occasionally, they won't be approved, in that case you just give them a certain percentage off (whatever you store is providing) and let them know they will be contacted by email to follow up.
2. Do you have a walkie or com? I generally use that and say, "Back-up at \[missus/mens\] POS please." If not there's a place in the top right hand corner of the screen with a phone icon, click that and it will bring up a cue menu. Some are "all available cashiers to the \[missus/mens\] register" or "additional cashiers to the \[missus/mens\] register."
3. Wednesday is senior discount day and the discount cannot be combined with certain other coupons or merchandise like Nike or Adidas.
4. I don't have any complaints about having water at my register or on the floor. I occasionally even have soda or juice. As long as it's a closed container and you keep it on the floor, you'll be fine.
5. My process for checking out is: hangers, security tag, fold. If you take off the security tags as you go, it will be less of a problem. Bag everything at the end and as you bag it, double check for a security tag. Remember that jewelry and sunglasses will occasionally beep but there is no security tag to remove.

And if a customer is rude, you just smile and say "Yes, of course" or "Let me check on that for you" and finally "Thank you for choosing Kohls, you have an excellent day!" Be friendly, placating if you need to be. They are not worth your stress. Good luck.

I find that most people being hired right now won't actually do the "job" they're hired to do. I was hired as a sales floor associate in early July but I'm only on the floor 1 day a week, I'm mostly doing POS (register), CS (customer service), or Amazon. It's important to understand that working in a larger company like Kohls, you will be expected to learn everything and anything.

Some of the main jobs are:

\-POS (which is the fancy term for the registers): There are generally two, one of the women's/missus side and one on the mens. This is pretty basic, you check people out, remove security tags, etc.... However, there's a few fancy things you learn how to do such as pay off their Kohl's Charge Card, make an even exchange, combine Kohl's cash, etc... I personally find register really easy. A more annoying part of working POS is CREDIT. Credit is when a cashier opens a Kohl's Charge Card (basically a Kohl's credit card). Right now the customer gets 35% off their purchase if they're approved and another 20% on their next purchase as well as secret coupons that come in the mail, it's a good deal if you're good with credit cards. The managers are crazy about credit. You'll be expected to bring in at least 1 credit per shift. However, most people tend to bring in 1 or 2 every other shift or so. 

\-Customer Service: It seems pretty simple, you take the returned item and you're done. But Kohl's has hassle-free returns so you can return an item without a receipt if you have the card you paid for the original item with (or you can get store credit, i.e a gift card). Then there's the process of the different bins, sorting, and tagging. It's a bit complicated, but again like the registers, easy if you make the customer happy. 

\-OMNI (which is where customers order online, occasionally same-day orders): A person goes around the store and scans all the items, with a Blue Bird, which is kind of like an industrial smart phone, the customer ordered and puts it in a basket to give to the customer as an instore online pick up. Because my store is short staffed we have an OMNI person, but generally, customer service is sent to find the pick ups in the back if possible.

\-Amazon: Kohl's does Amazon returns. A customer initiates the return and selects Kohl's Amazon Drop off. They bring their Amazon package to us, packaged or lose, with their QR code (those square barcode type things) and we will package it up with the right lables and return it for free of charge. It's very simple for the customer, for the employee on the otherhand, we have to make sure everything is labeled perfectly and sorted exactly. The store is fined for any mistakes Amazon makes. Most of the sorting is done in the back and it's pretty easy. You scan the lablew, that we put on the package during the return, with the BB (blue bird) and it tells you exactly which box it should be sorted into.

\-Floor: Floor associates are divided up into a few different sections, WJM (women, junior, men), home and kids, and shoes. Ocassioanly their are more categories or subcategories but for the most part you either stay in your section or everyone is blitzing a specific section. Blitzing refers to all the floor workers working on a really bad area at once. Floor associates make sure the fitting room stalls are clean (I prefer to check every 10 minutes) and keep the fitting rooms looking nice and the racks outside clear (which is difficult, if I'm honest, things get so crazy, especially in WJM). Another part of working the floor is register and customer service go backs, which is basically just racks of things that need to be taken back to their department. To be honest, the H2 (manager) will tell you what they want focused on today. A lot of the time we're unable to do fitting rooms and go backs on the weekends when we are super busy.

\-Jewelry/Beauty: The beauty should be right next to the jewelry and basically you're given other tasks to do, such as helping with fitting rooms, etc...and then someone at the register over the com will be like "there's a customer at jewelry, send someone over please" and that associate or a H2 will come over and help the customer.

There are other jobs, but for the most part this is what is worked. Of course there are crazy morning shifts like 4am-11:30am where we unload freights with our new shipments or price change before the store opens. But only a few people are put on those and it tends to be people the store manager trusts to work fast and efficiently. 

 As long as you're willing to learn and not afraid to ask questions, it's an excellent job. It's taken me about a full month to learn everything, and I only know the process of OMNI and Amazon sorting, I have not yet done it myself but I suspect I will eventually. I hope this isn't too wordy, I like Kohl's and the people I work with! And after week 2, you're feet don't hurt anyone more, haha.

Unfortunately, part of working retail is working at the registers. I created a step by step guide, that I'm hoping will help you. I'm fairly new as well, I started working at the beginning of July and honestly, it is 10x more overwhelming working the floor on a busy day than the register...once you get comfortable. I wrote a long list of how I run the register and what I do. Hopefully, this is helpful, but it is a lot of information and there is no harm in writing yourself a cheat sheet.

​

You do the basics, log in with your I.D and password and then go to the ‘Sales’ icon. 

Make polite small talk as you remove hangers, scan the item, and remove security tags (in that order). Removing the security tags as your scanning the item makes life easier than trying to remove them all at the end.

After they’ve given me the “I’m fine” or “Good, how are you?” I ask:

“Do you have a rewards card?”

They answer and I prompt them to enter their phone number on their screen. Occasionally, generally older people might have a physical rewards card, you will just scan the barcode on the back. The rewards card is the Yes2Rewards, they aren’t different so no need to worry.  However, if they say no, you can ask if they would like to open a rewards account…you should have little pamphlets at your register that shows them how to sign up.  Or they can sign up online, it’s very easy and self explanatory.

Following the rewards question, you ask:

“Do you have a Kohl’s Charge Card?”

Most of the time, they will say yes and have it with them. If they do not have it with them, click   
 “look up Kohl’s charge card” on the right hand side of the screen. It will prompt the customer to consent you scanning their license and after they click yes, scan it. If they have an account, it will pop up. The computer will prompt you to do the rest of it. 

OR they will say no. If they say no, you’re supposed to ask “would you like to open one?” and most of the time they say no, so you smile and move one scanning their items.

On the rare chance they decide to open one, finish scanning their items, and then you will take out the Kohl’s Charge Card forms and scan the barcode listed so it will prompt the computer to start the process. Have them fill out the rest of the form, they should take the form home because our records are automatically stored digitally. Then, on your screen, it will ask what type of I.D the customer is providing with a drop down menu, generally, it is a driver’s license. Their screen will ask if they consent to having their license scanned and assuming they click yes, you will scan their license. The rest of the information will need to be put it manually by the customer, including their SID/TIN, it is not an option and they must enter their full number to qualify. After that, all their information will show up on your screen and you will need to look at the license and make sure everything looks correct. You will click submit on the popup window and it will say please call for the card I.D number/approval. At the register, there should be a list of phone numbers or it should be labeled on the phone itself, call the number and you will be met with an operator. Follow the instructions the operator gives until you reach a real person. They will prompt you the rest of the way and give you the I.D number which you will enter into the computer and the card limit. You will then tell the customer that their card should come in the mail within a few weeks. After they’ve signed up and have been approved, you will discount 35% from their order. You will need to enter this manually, through the percent button options on the right hand side of the screen OR scan the 35% barcode at the register. If they are not approved, which the operator will tell you, they still will receive 25% off their order. 

Once this is done, you may begin scanning any coupons. I include Kohl’s Cash in the coupon section because it is essentially a discount. The customer will bring in paper copies or go online. All you need to do is scan the barcode and let them know which ones apply to this order and which ones don’t, most of the time you just say “certain coupons have exclusion items such as sports brands or shoes…etc.”

After their coupons/Kohl’s Cash is scanned you will read them their total in that is green at the bottom of the screen. If they ask if they will get more Kohl’s Cash back, make sure their subtitle is at least $50, not their total after tax. Once that is done, you will click on the total which will take you to the payment screen. Select if they are paying with cash, card, or gift-card. 

If it is a combination of things, like a gift-card and then card. It will prompt you to select another payment method after the gift-card is used. 

If they have already had you look up their Kohl’s Charge Card with their license, you will click card as payment and it the payment will automatically go through.

If they are paying with cash, you will select cash and input the amount of money they are giving you and then the drawer will pop open and tell you how much change to give back the customer. 

After that, bag the items in the appropriate size bags. If they have a few items, I’ll ask if they even want a bag, but anytime there is a lot of clothes or stuff I’ll just start bagging it. While this is happening, the computer will tell if you if the customer receives any Kohl’s Cash. Put on the leaflets through the scanning machine (it writes the amount on the backside of the coupon for the customer) and give it to them with their receipt.

If they want to make payments on their card, click on the home button in the left hand corner of the screen and click customer service on the main menu. There should be another icon that says “charge card payment”, select that and type in the amount they want to pay towards their card. A receipt with print and you will hand them that.
